rationale: This qualitative ethnographic and policy case study (based on archival research, 18 formal semi-structured interviews, and participant observation in 2010-2011) examines indigenous water justice in the Mataranka (Tindal Aquifer) Water Allocation Plan in Australia's Northern Territory. Using Fraser's tripartite justice framework, the study co-equally analyzes participatory water planning mechanisms and advisory committees (statutory Water Advisory Committees under NT water law, National Water Initiative participatory planning mandates, and the NLC-established Mataranka Traditional Owner Water Allocation Reference Group: participation_assistance), formal entitlement and native-title eligibility rules governing the Strategic Indigenous Reserve (comparing the Katherine Plan's native-title proof prerequisite against the Mataranka Plan's unconditional 25% commercial reserve: eligibility_status_documentation), and jurisdictional boundaries and statutory-customary governance coordination (boundedness of the Water Control District, narrow agency mandates excluding riparian vegetation, and articulation with local indigenous governance: institutional_structure_coordination). Because participatory planning representation and formal reserve/native-title entitlement rules are co-equally central empirical foci, primary_mechanism_family is participation_assistance and assigned_mechanism_label_with_multiple is multiple. Evaluated outcomes center on governance and regulatory planning intermediate outcomes (allocated commercial reserve shares and their deferral, formal plan recognition of indigenous cultural values, and stakeholder representation legitimacy: administrative_outcome).
